glance: 180 km to Sherpur by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
gajni-abokash-kendro.desc: Gajni, in Jhenaigati upazila, is a recreation area set among low hills covered in sal and mixed forest close to the Indian border. A lake with paddle boats, a hilltop watchtower, suspension bridges and picnic spots make it popular with families. From the tower you can see layered ridges stretching into Meghalaya. Wild elephants sometimes come down from the hills in this area, so stay on marked paths.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Dhaka or Mymensingh to Sherpur town, then a CNG or local bus to Jhenaigati and Gajni, about 1 hour.
Good to know
Go on a weekday to avoid picnic crowds; leave before dark because of wild elephants.

sherpur-indigenous-cultures.desc: The hill areas of Jhenaigati, Nalitabari and Sreebardi are home to Garo, Hajong, Koch, Barman and other indigenous communities. Many keep their own languages, matrilineal or clan-based customs, and harvest festivals such as the Garo Wangala. Weaving, bamboo craft and distinctive foods are part of village life. The best way to learn more is through a local guide or community-run homestay.
blocks: Good to know
Ask before photographing people or homes, and follow your hosts' customs.

glance: 180 km to Sherpur by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
ghagra-khan-bari-mosque.desc: In the Khan Bari of Ghagra Laskar village in Jhenaigati upazila stands a small mosque that an inscription over the door dates to 1028 AH, that is 1618–19. It has a single dome about 9 metres across, ten small minarets around the roof, and flowery patterns on the mihrab and inner walls, with lime-and-brick-dust walls about 1.2 metres thick. The Department of Archaeology has protected it since 1999. Next to it are the family eidgah and graveyard, and it makes a quiet stop on the way to Gajni.
blocks: How to get there
It is off the Sherpur–Jhenaigati road at Hatibandha union; take a CNG from Sherpur town toward Jhenaigati and ask for Ghagra Khan Bari.
Good to know
It is a working mosque, so dress modestly and ask before going inside.

glance: Rice markets and shops in Sherpur town
sherpur-tulshimala-rice.desc: Tulshimala is a fine, short-grained aromatic rice grown in Sherpur and registered as a Geographical Indication of the district. When cooked it gives off a sweet, nutty fragrance that fills the kitchen. It is the rice of choice for polao, kheer, payesh and festive pitha, and makes excellent khoi and muri. Buying a few kilos to take home is a good souvenir.

panihata-tarani-pahar.desc: Panihata, in Nalitabari upazila near the Indian border, is a small area of streams, sandbanks and low hills along the Bhogai river. Across the water the forested hills of Meghalaya rise steeply, making a striking backdrop. A Catholic mission nearby serves the local Garo community. It is far less crowded than Gajni and Madhutila.
blocks: How to get there
From Nalitabari take an auto or motorbike to Panihata, about 30–45 minutes.
Good to know
Do not cross towards the border; respect local communities and keep the riverbank clean.

glance: 180 km to Sherpur by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
madhutila-eco-park.desc: Madhutila Eco Park in Nalitabari upazila protects a patch of hill forest in the Garo foothills. Trails lead through sal and mixed woodland to a watchtower with views over the hills and border. There is a lake with boats and picnic spots. Early mornings are quiet and good for birds.
blocks: How to get there
From Sherpur town take a bus or CNG to Nalitabari, then an auto to Madhutila.
Good to know
Wild elephants roam the area; leave before dusk and follow staff advice.

mai-saheba-mosque.desc: Mai Saheba Mosque stands in the middle of Sherpur town, beside the government college. Its story goes back about 250 years, to a small abandoned room next to the Tin-Ani zamindars' rent office where a local woman used to pray. Legend says the zamindar sent an elephant to pull the room down, but the elephant sat down in front of it; finding the woman at prayer inside, he apologised and had a mosque built instead. The name Mai Saheba recalls her. Today it is a three-storey building with two tall minarets that holds more than 6,000 worshippers, and it is still being enlarged.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or auto anywhere in Sherpur town; it is on the Sherpur–Mymensingh road near Sherpur Government College.
Good to know
Visit outside prayer times and dress modestly. Fits easily into a day heading to Gajni or Madhutila in the Garo hills.

rajar-pahar.desc: Rajar Pahar in Sreebardi upazila is a hill with a broad, flat summit that rises above the surrounding plains and forest. Local legend links it to an old king who once ruled here, which gives the hill its name. A climb up gives views across paddy fields, streams and the hills of Meghalaya. Garo and other indigenous villages lie nearby, including at Babelakona.
blocks: How to get there
From Sherpur town take a bus or CNG to Sreebardi, then a local auto towards Karnajhora and Rajar Pahar.
Good to know
Wear good shoes, carry water and ask locals for the best path up.

sherpur-chhanar-payesh.desc: Chhanar payesh is made by cooking tiny balls of fresh chhana in milk that has been boiled down until thick and creamy. It is rich, mildly sweet and served cool. Once made by only a few shops, it is now sold by dozens across the district, and visitors carry tubs back to Dhaka. It is considered one of Sherpur's oldest food traditions.

glance: Cheap; about 120–130 BDT per kg in 2018
Sweet shops of Ghoshpatti in Sherpur town, such as Durgacharan, Nanda Gopal and Srikrishna Mistanna Bhandar
sherpur-dailer-amitti.desc: Dailer amitti is made from mashkalai (black gram) soaked and ground on a stone, mixed with atap rice flour, piped into coils, fried hot and dropped into sugar syrup. It looks like jalebi but is denser and chewier. Sherpur's sweet makers traditionally make it in autumn, and in Ramadan queues form for it at iftar time. The Ghoshpatti area of Sherpur town is the place, with old shops such as Durgacharan, Nanda Gopal and Srikrishna Mistanna Bhandar.
